transcript.content: Hello, I’m Dr. ___. What brings you in today?

Hi, Dr. ___. Well, it's... it's honestly a little embarrassing to talk about, but what brings me in is this issue I'm having where I just keep getting up. Like, physically leaving my seat when I am absolutely supposed to stay put. 

I'm a private investigator, and as you can probably imagine, my job involves a lot of sitting and listening. I have these initial client interviews where people are sitting across from my desk, pouring their hearts out about a cheating spouse or a missing business asset, and I'm supposed to be this stoic, attentive professional. But halfway through their story, I just... I have to stand up. I'll make up an excuse to check the window blinds, or grab a file, or I'll just start pacing the room while they're talking. 

And it's not just at work, either! I do some tutoring on the side, and the poor kids will be sitting there trying to work through a complicated equation, and I'm practically doing laps around the kitchen island instead of sitting next to them. Even at my book club—which is supposed to be relaxing, right? We're all sitting in someone's living room with wine and cheese, discussing a few chapters, and I'm the only one who keeps popping up from the sofa to look at a bookshelf or stand by the kitchen counter. 

It's getting to the point where people are really starting to notice. My clients give me these confused looks, the book club ladies make little passive-aggressive comments... they can all tell that I just can't sit and listen. It's really starting to affect how people see me professionally and personally, and I just don't know why I can't stay glued to a chair like everyone else.
Have you had this kind of difficulty since childhood?

Oh, absolutely. It's actually funny you ask that, because... well, I was just looking through this old box of keepsakes. My mom brought it over a few months ago when she was downsizing—you know how that goes, parents decide to declutter and suddenly you have a garage full of your own childhood macaroni art and old notebooks. But anyway, she had saved all my old grade-school report cards. Every single one of them. 

And reading through them, it was honestly like looking at a mirror of my life right now. The teachers, bless them, they always wrote the exact same thing year after year. They would always say that I was bright, which, you know, was nice of them to include, that I caught on to the reading and the math quickly. But then there was always this big caveat. They would write that I just couldn't stay in my seat, or that I had a terrible time waiting my turn to speak or do an activity. 

It was such a constant issue that my mother actually still jokes about it to this day. She thinks it is just the most hilarious thing, especially now that I'm a private investigator. She always tells people that I treated every single elementary school classroom like a crime scene that I just had to pace through. Like I was looking for clues over by the chalkboard or investigating the pencil sharpener instead of just sitting at my desk doing my worksheets like all the other normal kids. 

And I really did! I remember my fourth-grade teacher actually moved my desk right up next to hers, I think hoping that proximity would anchor me down somehow? But it never worked. I would still just pop up. I would go check the weather out the window, or go look at the class pet, or whatever excuse I could find to be out of that chair. So, yes, this definitely isn't some new quirk I developed as an adult. It has been there literally as long as I can remember, just this constant need to be on my feet and moving around.
Have you ever deliberately hurt, threatened, or seriously bullied other people?

Oh, gosh, no. No, definitely not. I mean, I know I have this whole issue with pacing and not being able to sit still, but I've never been aggressive or anything like that. Honestly, the idea of bullying someone just makes my stomach turn. 

Even when I was a kid—you know, back when I was constantly popping out of my seat and driving my teachers up the wall—I was never mean to the other kids. I might have been annoying because I was always interrupting or, you know, hovering over their desks when they were trying to do their spelling tests, but I never threatened anyone. I've always been more of a... a restless spirit, I guess you could say, rather than a malicious one. 

And in my line of work now as an investigator, I see people at their absolute worst. I deal with people who are angry, hurt, betrayed, and sometimes they want to lash out. But my job is to gather facts, not to intimidate people. I mean, sure, sometimes I have to ask tough questions or confront someone with evidence they don't want to see, but I always try to do it professionally. I would never deliberately hurt someone, physically or emotionally. It's just not in my nature at all. I might drive people crazy with my constant moving around, but I'm definitely not a bully.
Do you also have trouble paying attention to details or staying focused on tasks?

Honestly, no, not really. I mean, sure, my job requires a ton of attention to detail—sifting through financial records, cross-referencing timelines, analyzing surveillance footage. And I'm actually really good at that part! When I have a stack of bank statements in front of me and I need to find the one weird transaction that proves a spouse is hiding assets, I can zero right in on it. I don't miss those little details at all. 

It's just that while I'm doing it, I might be standing at the kitchen counter, or pacing back and forth with a highlighter in my hand, or listening to the audio files while I walk on the treadmill. But the focus itself? The ability to actually lock onto the task and get the work done? That's never been the problem. I can hyper-focus on a case for hours, tracking down every little lead, making sure every single 'i' is dotted and 't' is crossed. 

Even when I'm tutoring, I don't lose the thread of the math problem. I know exactly where the kid made the mistake in the equation, I'm just pointing it out while I'm doing a lap around the dining room table. And at book club, I know exactly what chapter we're discussing and the nuances of the characters' motivations—I'm just contributing to the conversation while I'm examining a knick-knack on the mantelpiece. 

So, yeah, it's not a focus issue. I don't feel like my mind is wandering off or that I'm forgetting what I'm supposed to be doing. It's strictly this physical... this intense physical urge to just get up and move. The mental part of my job, the detail-oriented stuff, that's actually the part I excel at. It's just the sitting still while I do it that seems to be completely impossible for me.
